analysis.one_liner: Requires federal rules so permitted projects cause no net loss of U.S. wetlands.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in a House subcommittee at the end of the 102nd Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Army and the Environmental Protection Agency to write rules guaranteeing that permitted construction and development activities do not reduce the total acres of wetlands that existed in the United States as of June 1989, or their functions and values. It also would have created an accounting system to track wetland acreage and required a report to Congress on any wetland losses since 1989. It was introduced by Rep. Barbara Boxer and never advanced past a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who relies on wetlands for flood protection, cleaner water, wildlife habitat, and groundwater recharge. A binding no-net-loss rule means developers who destroy wetlands must replace or restore an equal amount, keeping the public's share of these natural flood and water-filtration systems from shrinking over time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public that relies on wetlands

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require a federal program ensuring no net loss in the total acres of U.S. wetlands that existed on June 8, 1989, and no reduction in their functions and values from permitted activities.

It would mandate a wetland acreage accounting system to accurately measure total wetland acres and changes caused by permitted projects, and a report to Congress on losses since June 8, 1989 and actions needed to comply.

analysis.who_pays: Landowners, developers, and home builders who fill or build on wetlands would face stricter permitting and the cost of replacing any wetlands they destroy. Those costs would tend to show up in the price of land and construction in wetland-rich areas.
analysis.who_pays_short: Developers and landowners building on wetlands

drawbacks.text: A strict no-net-loss standard would raise permitting and mitigation costs for landowners and developers, and those costs are ultimately passed on in housing and construction prices in areas with wetlands.

The bill requires that permitted activities cause no reduction in the 'functions and value' of wetlands as well as acreage, a standard that is difficult to measure precisely and could invite disputes over how replacement projects are judged.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — keeping the nation's wetlands from shrinking, with their flood control, water filtration, and habitat value — is broad and long-lasting. The cost falls on a narrower group, developers and landowners, and on homebuyers in wetland-rich areas to a modest degree. The main design weakness is the hard-to-measure 'functions and value' standard, but the core acreage accounting is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee referred it to a water resources subcommittee three days after it was introduced, and no markup or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Boxer introduced the Wetlands Preservation Act in the House on March 18, 1992.
It was referred to the House Committee on Public Works and Transportation the same day, with one Democratic cosponsor.
On March 30, 1992 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources, and the record shows no further action before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Developers and landowners who fill wetlands are better off because no binding no-net-loss rule was enacted; the public never gained the acreage guarantee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Developers and landowners, not the public

for.name: Rep. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before the House, proposing a mandatory no-net-loss wetlands program under the Clean Water Act.

for.name: 1 of 1 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew only one cosponsor in the House.

against.name: House Committee on Public Works and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and never held a markup or brought it to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never measured; the bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and home builders
industries.note: A binding no-net-loss rule would make destroying wetlands under a Section 404 permit far more costly, requiring replacement acreage and functions. Their interest in weak wetland rules runs against the public's interest in keeping flood control and water filtration intact.

The bill covers permitted activities under the Clean Water Act's Section 404, the pathway used to convert wetlands for farming, forestry, and building. Farmers and timber operators would face tighter limits on draining or filling wetlands.
